## Overview {#sec-overview}

This project applies a Mendelian randomization (MR) approach to investigate whether omega-3 fatty acid balance has causal effects on Alzheimer’s disease–related phenotypes. Genetic variants associated with three omega-3–related exposures—the ratio of omega-3 fatty acids to total fatty acids, the ratio of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) to total fatty acids, and the ratio of omega-6 to omega-3 fatty acids—were used as instrumental variables.

Summary-level genome-wide association study (GWAS) data were analyzed for six Alzheimer’s disease–related outcomes, including disease progression score, hippocampal volume, cortical amyloid deposition, average cortical thickness, and left and right caudate volumes. The inverse-variance weighted method was used as the primary analysis, with weighted median and MR Egger methods as sensitivity analyses.

This project aims to clarify whether genetic predisposition to higher omega-3 status is causally associated with brain structural changes and Alzheimer’s disease–related pathology.

All analyses were conducted in R, and the complete reproducible workflow is available at: [BMIN5030_Final_Project/final_project_Yucheng_12.31.2025.qmd at master · richardhuang929/BMIN5030_Final_Project](https://github.com/richardhuang929/BMIN5030_Final_Project/blob/master/final_project_Yucheng_12.31.2025.qmd)

## Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Omega-3 fatty acids are essential components of neuronal cell membranes and play an important role in brain development and maintenance. Among them, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is highly concentrated in the brain and is involved in synaptic function, membrane fluidity, and neuroinflammatory regulation. Experimental studies suggest that omega-3 fatty acids may have neuroprotective effects and may slow neurodegenerative processes.

Observational studies have reported associations between higher omega-3 intake and reduced risk of cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, these findings are inconsistent and may be influenced by confounding factors such as diet, lifestyle, and socioeconomic status. In addition, reverse causation cannot be excluded, as individuals with early neurodegeneration may change their dietary habits.

AD is characterized by progressive brain atrophy, amyloid-β accumulation, and deterioration of subcortical and cortical structures. Brain imaging phenotypes, such as cortical thickness, hippocampal volume, and caudate volume, provide important insights into disease progression and neurodegeneration. Understanding whether omega-3 fatty acids have a causal influence on these phenotypes may help clarify their role in AD pathology.

MR uses genetic variants as proxies for lifelong exposure and can reduce bias from confounding and reverse causation. In this study, we used a two-sample MR study design to examine the causal effects of omega-3 fatty acid balance, with a particular focus on DHA, on multiple AD–related phenotypes.

## Methods {#sec-methods}

A two-sample MR design was applied to evaluate the causal effects of omega-3–related exposures on AD–related outcomes. Genetic variants associated with omega-3 fatty acid balance were used as instrumental variables.

### **Data Sources**

GWAS summary statistics were obtained for three omega-3–related exposures: the ratio of omega-3 fatty acids to total fatty acids, the ratio of DHA to total fatty acids, and the ratio of omega-6 to omega-3 fatty acids. These ratios reflect long-term differences in omega-3 status and fatty acid balance. Independent single nucleotide polymorphisms significantly associated with each exposure were selected as instrumental variables.

Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with each fatty acid ratio at genome-wide significance were selected as instrumental variables. Linkage disequilibrium clumping was applied to ensure independence among instruments prior to Mendelian randomization analyses.

Six AD–related phenotypes were included as outcomes: AD progression score, hippocampal volume in AD, cortical amyloid deposition in AD, average cortical thickness, left caudate volume, and right caudate volume. These outcomes represent key aspects of AD pathology and brain structural changes.

All outcome GWAS data were derived from large population-based studies of European ancestry. These outcomes were selected to capture both clinical-level cognitive performance and biological markers across different stages of AD, allowing a more comprehensive assessment of the potential causal effects of fatty acid composition on cognitive function and AD-related phenotypes.

### Mendelian Randomization Design

A two-sample MR framework was employed. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with each omega-3 fatty acids exposure at genome-wide significance (P \< 5×10⁻⁸) were selected as candidate instrumental variables. Linkage disequilibrium clumping was applied to ensure independence among instruments. Weak instruments were excluded using F-statistics, with SNPs having F \< 10 removed prior to analysis.

Primary causal estimates were obtained using the inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method. Heterogeneity among genetic instruments was assessed using Cochran’s Q test. When evidence of heterogeneity was detected (P \< 0.05), the IVW random-effects model was applied. When heterogeneity was not significant (P ≥ 0.05), the IVW fixed-effects model was used. Additional MR methods, including weighted median and MR-Egger regression, were performed as sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the findings.

### Sensitivity Analyses

Several sensitivity analyses and graphical diagnostics were performed to assess the robustness of the MR results. MR-Egger intercept tests were conducted to evaluate the presence of directional horizontal pleiotropy. Leave-one-out analyses were used to examine whether the overall causal estimates were driven by any single genetic variant.

Scatter plots were generated to visualize the associations between SNP effects on the exposure and the corresponding effects on each outcome, with regression lines representing different MR methods. In addition, MR effect plots were used to compare causal estimates derived from inverse-variance weighted, weighted median, and MR-Egger approaches. Consistency across these analyses was used to support the stability of the MR findings.

All analyses were conducted in R using the TwoSampleMR package. Code was written to ensure reproducibility and transparency, with detailed comments explaining each processing and analysis step.

```{r}
exposure_dat_omega_3 <- extract_instruments(c("ebi-a-GCST90092932"),clump = F,p1 = 5e-08)
exposure_dat_omega_3 <- clump_data(exposure_dat_omega_3,clump_kb = 10000, clump_r2 = 0.001)
calc_fstat <- function(dat,
                       beta_col = "beta.exposure",
                       se_col   = "se.exposure",
                       f_thresh = 10,
                       drop_na  = TRUE) {
  
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(dat))
  if (!all(c(beta_col, se_col) %in% names(dat))) {
    stop("Missing columns: ", paste(setdiff(c(beta_col, se_col), names(dat)), collapse = ", "))
  }
  
  out <- dat %>%
    mutate(
      F_stat = (.data[[beta_col]] / .data[[se_col]])^2
    )
  
  if (drop_na) {
    out <- out %>% filter(is.finite(F_stat))
  }
  
  out_keep <- out %>% filter(F_stat >= f_thresh)
  
  summary_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
    n_before = nrow(out),
    n_after  = nrow(out_keep),
    n_dropped = nrow(out) - nrow(out_keep),
    f_threshold = f_thresh,
    F_min = min(out$F_stat, na.rm = TRUE),
    F_median = stats::median(out$F_stat, na.rm = TRUE),
    F_mean = mean(out$F_stat, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
  
  list(
    data_with_F = out,
    data_filtered = out_keep,
    summary = summary_tbl
  )
}

res <- calc_fstat(exposure_dat_omega_3, f_thresh = 10)

res$summary
exposure_dat_omega_3 <- res$data_filtered

weak_snps <- anti_join(res$data_with_F, exposure_dat_omega_3, by = intersect(names(res$data_with_F), names(exposure_dat_omega_3)))
weak_snps %>% select(SNP, beta.exposure, se.exposure, F_stat) %>% arrange(F_stat)
```

```{r}
res <- mr(dat_ft,method_list = c("mr_egger_regression","mr_weighted_median","mr_ivw_fe","mr_ivw_mre"))
res$lower <- res$b - 1.96 * res$se
res$upper <- res$b + 1.96 * res$se
res$OR <- exp(res$b)
res
mr_heterogeneity(dat_ft)
mr_pleiotropy_test(dat_ft)
res_single <- mr_singlesnp(dat_ft)
res_loo <- mr_leaveoneout(dat_ft)
mr_leaveoneout_plot(res_loo)
p1 <- mr_scatter_plot(res, dat_ft)
res_single <- mr_singlesnp(dat_ft)
mr_funnel_plot(res_single)
mr_scatter_plot(res, dat_ft)
```

```{r}
  out <- dat %>%
    mutate(
      F_stat = (.data[[beta_col]] / .data[[se_col]])^2
    )
  
  if (drop_na) {
    out <- out %>% filter(is.finite(F_stat))
  }
  
  out_keep <- out %>% filter(F_stat >= f_thresh)
  
  summary_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
    n_before = nrow(out),
    n_after  = nrow(out_keep),
    n_dropped = nrow(out) - nrow(out_keep),
    f_threshold = f_thresh,
    F_min = min(out$F_stat, na.rm = TRUE),
    F_median = stats::median(out$F_stat, na.rm = TRUE),
    F_mean = mean(out$F_stat, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
  
  list(
    data_with_F = out,
    data_filtered = out_keep,
    summary = summary_tbl
  )
}

res <- calc_fstat(exposure_dat_n6n3, f_thresh = 10)

res$summary
exposure_dat_n6n3 <- res$data_filtered

weak_snps <- anti_join(res$data_with_F, exposure_dat_n6n3, by = intersect(names(res$data_with_F), names(exposure_dat_n6n3)))
weak_snps %>% select(SNP, beta.exposure, se.exposure, F_stat) %>% arrange(F_stat)
```

## Results {#sec-results}

For the three omega-3–related exposure traits—ratio of omega-3 fatty acids to total fatty acids, ratio of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) to total fatty acids, and ratio of omega-6 fatty acids to omega-3 fatty acids—independent genetic variants were selected as instrumental variables after standard quality control procedures. All instruments showed adequate strength, and no strong evidence of directional pleiotropy was detected based on sensitivity analyses. Heterogeneity tests guided the choice between fixed-effects and random-effects IVW models.

### Ratio of omega-3 fatty acids to total PUFAs

For the ratio of omega-3 fatty acids to total fatty acids, IVW analyses showed no statistically significant associations with AD progression score, hippocampal volume, or cortical amyloid deposition. However, a modest positive association with average cortical thickness was observed. In addition, negative associations with caudate volume were suggested, particularly for the right caudate volume, where IVW estimates reached statistical significance. Weighted median results for caudate volume were statistically significant and showed consistent directions.

These findings suggest that omega-3 fatty acids may be more strongly related to brain structural features than to classical AD pathological markers. The consistent negative associations with caudate volume across IVW and weighted median analyses support the robustness of this result. In contrast, the lack of association with amyloid deposition and hippocampal volume indicates that omega-3 effects may not directly target core AD pathology.

### Ratio of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) to total PUFAs

For the ratio of DHA to total fatty acids, IVW analyses indicated no significant associations with hippocampal volume or cortical amyloid deposition. In contrast, average cortical thickness showed a consistent positive association across IVW, weighted median, and MR Egger analyses, suggesting a robust relationship. Negative associations between DHA and caudate volume were observed, with weighted median estimates reaching statistical significance, while IVW estimates showed similar but weaker effects. In addition, the IVW fixed-effects analysis showed a positive association between DHA and Alzheimer’s disease progression score.

Compared with total omega-3 fatty acids, DHA showed more consistent associations with cortical thickness, highlighting its potential importance for cortical integrity. The agreement across multiple MR methods strengthens the credibility of this finding. Although IVW estimates for caudate volume were not always statistically significant, the consistent direction and significant weighted median results suggest that DHA may influence subcortical brain structures.

### Ratio of omega-6 to omega-3 fatty acids

For the ratio of omega-6 to omega-3 fatty acids, IVW analyses did not identify significant associations with hippocampal volume or cortical amyloid deposition. However, positive associations with caudate volume were observed, particularly for the right caudate volume, where both IVW random-effects and weighted median estimates were statistically significant.

These results suggest that a higher omega-6 to omega-3 ratio may be associated with unfavorable changes in caudate volume. The consistency between IVW and weighted median estimates supports the robustness of this association. Similar to the omega-3 and DHA analyses, no clear associations were observed with amyloid-related outcomes, further indicating that fatty acid balance may primarily affect brain structure rather than amyloid pathology.

### Overall interpretation

Across all analyses, IVW results showed limited evidence for strong causal effects on classical AD pathological markers. However, consistent associations were observed for brain structural phenotypes, particularly cortical thickness and caudate volume. In several instances, weighted median estimates were statistically significant when IVW estimates were not, suggesting that these findings are relatively robust to potential pleiotropy.

Taken together, these patterns suggest that omega-3 fatty acids, especially DHA, may influence brain structural integrity rather than directly modifying amyloid accumulation. The consistency of effect directions across MR methods supports the biological plausibility of these associations, while the generally modest effect sizes indicate that omega-3–related effects are likely to be subtle.

## Conclusion

In this MR study, we investigated the potential causal effects of omega-3 fatty acid balance, with a particular focus on DHA, on AD–related phenotypes. Overall, IVW analyses showed limited evidence for strong causal effects on classical AD pathological markers, such as hippocampal volume and cortical amyloid deposition. However, consistent associations were observed for brain structural measures, especially average cortical thickness and caudate volume.

From a biological perspective, these findings are plausible. Omega-3 fatty acids, particularly DHA, are major components of neuronal cell membranes and contribute to membrane fluidity and synaptic function. Higher DHA levels may help maintain cortical structure by supporting neuronal integrity and reducing age-related cortical thinning. In addition, omega-3 fatty acids are known to have anti-inflammatory properties, which may indirectly protect brain tissue from chronic neuroinflammation that contributes to neurodegeneration.

The observed associations with caudate volume suggest that omega-3 fatty acids may also influence subcortical brain regions involved in cognitive and motor processes. Changes in fatty acid composition could affect neuronal metabolism and signaling in these regions, leading to measurable structural differences. In contrast, the lack of strong associations with amyloid deposition implies that omega-3 fatty acids may not directly modify amyloid-related pathways, but instead exert their effects through structural and neuroprotective mechanisms.

In summary, this study suggests that omega-3 fatty acids, especially DHA, may play a modest role in maintaining brain structural integrity rather than directly altering core Alzheimer’s disease pathology. Further studies using larger genetic datasets and more detailed neuroimaging phenotypes are needed to better understand the biological pathways linking omega-3 fatty acids to brain structure and Alzheimer’s disease progression.
